Expectation1: Support each other emotionally during tough times
Situation1: One sibling has just received some very difficult news and is deeply distressed by it.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story: I sat on the edge of my bed, my phone buzzing with messages from the advocacy group. They wanted me to present the latest case of unfair treatment at tomorrow’s meeting—another story to add to the growing list, another chance to push for change. But just down the hall, my stepbrother’s muffled sobs seeped through the door. He’d just found out his biological father wasn’t coming to visit, again. As his step-sibling, I was supposed to be there for him, to listen and offer comfort, to remind him he wasn’t alone. But as an advocate, I was expected to be focused, prepared, and relentless, ready to speak up for those who couldn’t. My mind raced between the two worlds—one demanding my empathy and presence, the other my determination and voice. I felt torn, guilt pressing in from both sides, unsure which role needed me more in this moment.
